headline: Australian consumer sentiment improving but remains at historically low levels, with inflation expectations still elevated
reasoning: Consumer sentiment is still pessimistic overall and near 50-year lows, but there has been improvement since bottoming out following the Middle East conflict. Consumers are becoming more optimistic about family finances and the broader economy, suggesting a levels-versus-trend dynamic. Inflation expectations remain strong, partly influenced by the rolling out of fuel excise tax discounts.
quote: So with consumers of course, we're seeing that they're quite pessimistic in terms of overall sentiment. But we are seeing an improvement in several areas. So we are seeing consumers becoming more optimistic in terms of how they're feeling about their family finances as well as around the economy. Um, I think this is a levels versus trend story. So we are seeing improvements since bottoming out following the Middle East conflict. But it does look like sentiment is overall improving while still remaining pessimistic of course. Still on very low levels.
episode_title: Inflation may look cooler, but Westpac sees heat underneath

headline: Westpac sees trimmed mean inflation at 3.5% for July, still above RBA target, with core pressures remaining sticky
reasoning: Sharma expects trimmed mean CPI of 0.4% in July, a pick-up from June's 0.3%, with the year-ended core rate at 3.5% — still above the RBA's 2-3% target band. Broad-based price pressures persist across multiple categories. While June quarter CPI came in softer than expected, it remains strong overall and not consistent with the RBA's target. The disinflationary impulse is expected to come as the economy slows and labour market slack increases.
quote: For trimmed mean, we're expecting a 0.4%. That's a bit of a pick up from June where we got 0.3%, but we are expecting a slight dip in year ended. And so therefore, what would be the annual core rate that you're looking for? So we're looking for a 3.5%. So that's still above what the RBA wants.
episode_title: Inflation may look cooler, but Westpac sees heat underneath

headline: New dwelling cost inflation running at 5.7% year-ended and expected to remain persistent, driven by materials costs and competition from data centre construction
reasoning: New housing inflation is one of the key pressure points in the CPI basket and has significant weight, suggesting persistence in trimmed mean inflation. Materials prices have been rising due to Middle East conflict. There is also competition for resources between nonresidential building (particularly data centre build-out) and residential building. Westpac expects a 0.4% rise in new dwelling costs for July, taking the year-ended rate to 5.7%, with disinflation from there expected to be slow.
quote: New housing inflation is, of course, one of the key pressure points in the CPI basket currently. It doesn't bode well for trimmed mean inflation because it does suggest there will be some persistence there just given its weight in the CPI basket. So the key things that are affecting it there is what's happening in the Middle East that's seeing materials price increase by quite a lot. We're also seeing some competition for resources between nonresidential building and residential building, particularly as data center build out phase expands. So we expect a 0.4% rise in new dwelling costs for July. That will take the year ended rate to 5.7. And the disinflation from there is quite slow to progress.
episode_title: Inflation may look cooler, but Westpac sees heat underneath

headline: Forecasts July CPI headline at 3.3% year-ended, well below June's 3.8%, driven largely by base effects in electricity prices
reasoning: Neha Sharma expects a 0.8% monthly lift in July CPI but a significant drop in the year-ended rate to 3.3% from 3.8% in June. The main driver of the decline is base effects from strong electricity price rises last year not repeating. Upward pressures include auto fuel (excise discount rolling from 32c to 16c), seasonal holiday travel increases, and water and property rates. Electricity, via lower default market offers in most states, is expected to be the main offset.
quote: So in terms of the July CPI data that's coming out tomorrow, we're expecting a 0.8% lift in the month. That's quite a strong number at face value. But the year ended pace, we are actually expecting quite a significant drop to 3.3% from 3.8% in June. And a lot of this is due to base effects. So we saw electricity prices last year come up quite strongly, and we're not expecting the same level of impulse there.
episode_title: Inflation may look cooler, but Westpac sees heat underneath

headline: Westpac base case is no further RBA rate hikes, with cuts expected from August 2027, but upside inflation risks remain
reasoning: Westpac's base case is for no further rate hikes, with rate cuts expected from August 27 onwards. However, there is a risk of further hikes if upside inflation risks materialise, as the RBA has flagged openness to hiking if necessary. Sharma expects the unemployment rate to move towards 5% as economic slack builds, which should help bring inflation back towards the RBA target band. The disinflationary impulse is seen as coming primarily from a slowing economy and a looser labour market.
quote: Well our base case is now for no further rate hikes. Um, and until August 27th where we're expecting cuts from then onwards. But there is of course a risk for further hikes. The RBA has said that they're open to further hikes if upside risks to inflation materialise. We don't necessarily see that happening. Of course June quarter CPI came in a bit softer than expected. It's still strong overall and like you said, not consistent with the RBA's target band for July.
episode_title: Inflation may look cooler, but Westpac sees heat underneath
